headline: Eagles in the Arena: After state title loss, Bakersfield Christian HS looks to right the wrongs of the past
content:
The Daily Brief

Eagles in the Arena: After state title loss, Bakersfield Christian HS looks to right the wrongs of the past

Good morning, Bakersfield. It’s Friday, August 14, 2026, and we’re starting the day with a look at the night that was — from a high-speed DUI south of the Grapevine to a welfare check for a woman seen crying for help in a red pickup. Today’s high will reach 95°, with an overnight low around 67°, and air quality is moderate at AQI 59. Let’s get you caught up.

The Kern Overnight

The night opened quietly enough, with a traffic unit requested around 9:10 p.m. for the 600 block of 33rd Street. But by 9:23 p.m., dispatchers were sending city units to White Lane for a road-rage disturbance involving a blue Honda with paper plates and a white pickup, both repeatedly stopping and blocking the eastbound roadway. The incident drew no further update on the air. Around 10:33 p.m., a white 2001 Dodge van with California plates was reported stolen on Kentucky Street; officers took the report, and no arrests were announced. The night’s most serious call came around 11:34 p.m., when Bakersfield police broadcast an attempt-to-locate and welfare check after a caller described an older-model red truck at South Chester Avenue and Belle Terrace — a male hanging out the driver’s window, a female crying and saying she needed help. The truck was last seen traveling southbound, and the broadcast went out citywide. Fire crews were comparatively quiet, handling a residential alarm on Greenview Lane around 11 p.m. that amounted to nothing and a vehicle accident that drew an engine, battalion, and rescue unit before the air went quiet. Just after midnight, a theft from a space at a mobile home park on Barlow Road was reported, with a loss estimated near $3,900 and a suspect named. And shortly before 3 a.m., a traffic collision in the Flying J truck stop parking lot at Frazier Park saw a burgundy Freightliner hit by a red Peterbilt, with the other party denying involvement. CHP was investigating the hit-and-run claim as the feed moved on.

Today's weather

Today’s high will reach 95° under sunny skies, with a low tonight around 67°. It’s currently 77° at Meadows Field (KBFL), and no active weather alerts are in effect for Kern County. Air quality is moderate at AQI 59.

Top stories

KGET 17 reports that Bakersfield Christian High School’s football team is looking to right the wrongs of last year’s state title loss as they gear up for the new season. The Eagles are working to build on their experience and come back stronger, with a focus on teamwork and determination.

23ABC tells us that Bakersfield’s police and fire chiefs presented their Fourth of July reports during a Friday meeting, revealing both progress and ongoing concerns about fireworks-related incidents in the city. Kevin Albertson, Chief of the Bakersfield Fire Department, said the holiday brought serious consequences for people across the state. A total of 106 citations were issued by the Bakersfield Police and Fire departments combined in relation to the holiday. Compared to 2025, fire-related responses to both departments dropped 6% in 2026. Despite the decrease, residents and officials say more work remains. Bakersfield City Councilman Eric Arias said stronger policies are in the works.

23ABC also shares that Carlos Baldovinos, executive director of the Mission at Kern County, traveled to San Diego on August 12 to celebrate the public release of a federal best practices toolkit aimed at addressing addiction treatment within the homeless community — a project he helped build from the ground up. Baldovinos was among roughly 22 professionals from across the country who gathered in Washington, D.C., in the spring to work with the Trump administration, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the nation’s drug czar to develop the toolkit. The toolkit outlines best practices for working with individuals dealing with addiction within the homeless population, covering topics including program length, transitional housing, long-term mentorship, and workforce development.

KGET 17 reports that Kern County supervisors are exploring a proposal that would place Kern and dozens of other counties in a new state, separate from coastal California. Kern County District 3 Supervisor Jeff Flores said the effort is about making sure the region’s industries and way of life are taken seriously by state leaders. An analysis presented to the board found the proposed inland state would account for only about 15 percent of California’s current real GDP. CSU Bakersfield economics professor Richard Gearhart said that number tells a stark story about what separation would actually mean for the region.

The Kern Overnight

The night’s biggest incident was a grass fire that broke out just after 1 a.m. about 2 miles east of the county dump and north of the railroad tracks. First reports put it at 3–5 acres, but it grew to 5–10 acres as units arrived. Crews dispatched to what they called the Apollo Incident included Engine 345, Water Tender 12, dozers, a safety officer, and helicopter 409. They worked access through corral roads, and Union Pacific train traffic was held while they mopped up.

Around 2:22 a.m., a fire in an alley near 9th & K streets spread into a garage and drew the Station 1 assignment: Engine 1, Truck 1, Rescue 1, Battalion 1, and Engine 6. Just before 2:20 a.m., a burglary in progress sent units searching for a suspect described as a white male, 5-foot-11, about 150 pounds, in a white tank top and black gym shorts. He was last seen riding a blue beach cruiser and exiting onto Union Avenue. Around 12:24 a.m., units responded to 21st & O streets for a person in crisis, reportedly nude with a shirt draped over them and possibly in the middle of a psychiatric episode.

The log also noted a few other incidents: at 22:01, unknown subjects in a blue Honda dropped items off at a vacant residence on Madera Street in Maricopa, then left southbound. At 22:07, a report came in of a 6-year-old possibly locked out of a residence in the 700 block of Jefferson Street. At 23:00, a disturbance was reported at a business in the 2700 block of White Lane. At 23:46, a vehicle was reported not stopping on Highway 99 toward the 223, with a possible pursuit in progress. Top stories

23ABC reports that college costs continue to surge, with the average family spending more than $34,000 on college this past school year—a sharp 10% jump from the year before. Financial expert Jennifer Finetti, director of student advocacy at ScholarshipOwl, says a combination of factors is driving tuition higher, including changes in federal research funding and a decline in international students. "Plus, of course, inflation. Just like it makes costs for all of us go up, it also makes the cost go up for colleges as well. All the suppliers and things they need to keep running," Finetti said. Finetti says one of the biggest mistakes parents make is waiting too long to have honest conversations about what their family can realistically afford—and what students may need to contribute. "That's something I think parents can talk to their kids about, and to say 'Hey, integrate applying for scholarships into your life. If you want to go to college, you need to do your part,'" Finetti said. Finetti also says families shouldn't rule out community college, even for students who have good grades and could go straight to a four-year university. "They can get two years done at a very low cost, living at home, and then they can transfer to complete their bachelor's degree," Finetti said. For families considering student loans, there are major new rules to watch. Finetti says changes that took effect July 1 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act give new borrowers fewer federal repayment options. One plan can tie monthly payments to a borrower's income, meaning payments could climb.

According to 23ABC, a fake government form is circulating in AI-generated videos online, falsely promising seniors they can freeze their property taxes or stop paying school-bond charges, and Kern County officials say it is already generating calls and walk-ins at the assessor-recorder's office. The videos promote a form called "1098-SR," claiming people over 65 can use it to eliminate certain tax obligations. Kern County Assessor-Recorder Laura Avila says the form does not exist. "In the last couple weeks, we've been receiving phone calls and customers—or taxpayers, property owners—coming into our counter and asking to fill out this form 1098-SR," Avila said. Avila says her office searched for the form and could not find any federal program tied to it. While some other states offer similar property tax programs, California does not. When her staff explains the form is not real, residents are often upset because they heard about it from friends or saw it in videos online and often believe they are being denied. Avila says some of the videos appear on YouTube and are labeled as AI-generated at the bottom. The videos are broad, she says, targeting multiple states without specifying which programs apply where, and they feature what appear to be real people explaining programs that do not exist in California. Avila says her office has not confirmed anyone losing money or being asked to pay, which is why she is calling this a preventive advisory. But she is concerned about what could come next. "My fear is that the next phase of this will be somebody soliciting seniors."

KGET 17 tells us that early heat waves are shrinking Kern County pistachio harvests, raising prices for consumers. Hot summers are nothing new to Kern County, but early extreme heat waves this year are taking a serious toll on pistachio crops, shrinking harvests across the region. Fewer blooms on trees can mean a sharper drop in fruit production, leaving growers with fewer pistachios to harvest. LaBorde's business manager Jonathan Romero says pistachio trees naturally follow a cycle of higher-yield years followed by lower-yield years. Growers are currently facing one of those lower-production seasons, with extreme heat adding even more pressure. "Not only are we faced with a low crop yield this year, but we're also being affected by inflation." Romero says higher market prices help even out the disparity for farmers when numbers rise on shelves. He says he is worried about how this is affecting smaller-scale pistachio farmers who rely solely on a handful of nut varieties. "Pistachios might be a bit more expensive this year, but you're helping the growers—the local growers, family farms; I think that's what they should all take into consideration," Romero said. Dr. Richard Gearhart, a professor of economics at California State University, says that when a product becomes rare, local and overseas shoppers must compete to buy it, which drives up the price for everyone domestically and internationally. According to the United States Department of Agriculture, the estimated projected yield for California's total pistachio harvest sits at around 600 to 900 million pounds this year, compared to last year's harvest of 1.63 billion pounds.

Preliminary information indicates two unknown suspects arrived at the Capri Liquors in the 100 block of Perkins Avenue and confronted the victim inside the Capri Laundromat, which is adjacent to the gas pumps. An argument led to one of the suspects producing a firearm and shooting the victim multiple times. The two suspects then fled the area in an unknown vehicle. McFarland Police Department detectives are actively working the scene and gathering investigative information. Police say there is no current threat to the community, but the public is advised to avoid the area until the scene is processed. Anyone with information about this investigation is asked to call Detective Galvan or Detective Cazares at 661-792-2121.

The mayor’s statement comes after a 15-year-old suspect was arrested in connection with the incident. She urged anyone with information to come forward and cooperate with law enforcement. The mayor’s office is working with local authorities to ensure a thorough investigation and to support the affected families and community members.

According to 23ABC, Kern County water agencies are taking early action against golden mussel threat to water supply. Golden mussels remain a growing threat to California's water supply, but water agencies in Kern County are taking early action to stay ahead of the invasive species before it can disrupt water delivery. On Tuesday, a round table was held in Bakersfield, bringing together Representative Vince Fong, local water agencies and other stakeholders to discuss ways to fight back against golden mussels. Andrea Sealock with SePRO Water attended the event and said interagency cooperation was a central theme. Sealock pointed to Arvin Edison Water Storage District as an example of a district acting responsibly after it detected golden mussels in its system in December 2025. SePRO worked with Arvin Edison on a treatment program using an EPA-approved, copper-based treatment while monitoring the system. Sealock said the work is showing promising results. SePRO is also currently working with multiple water districts throughout Kern County.

Bakersfield Now reports that a "severe vermin infestation" has shut down Pho Hut on California Avenue after roaches were found. The restaurant was closed by health inspectors after a routine inspection uncovered a significant rodent and cockroach infestation. The closure comes after inspectors found live and dead roaches throughout the facility, as well as rodent droppings and gnaw marks. The restaurant will remain closed until it addresses the vermin issues and passes a re-inspection.

KGET 17 tells us the City of Bakersfield is set to finalize the purchase of the Bank of America building. The city council is expected to approve the final purchase agreement for the downtown building at its next meeting. The building is expected to house the city’s finance, administrative services, and parks and recreation departments.

The 15-year-old teen charged with the shooting death of another made his first court appearance in Juvenile Court on Wednesday morning. Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer identified the suspect as Gabriel Torres Reyes. A judge ordered Reyes to remain in custody on a first-degree murder charge in the death of 17-year-old Levi Brown, who was shot at a football game at Independence High School last Friday. Prosecutors charged Reyes with premeditated, first-degree murder, along with a gang enhancement and an allegation that he personally used a firearm causing Brown's death. Reyes denied the charges and allegations — the juvenile court equivalent of a not-guilty plea. Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer said California law requires the case to remain in juvenile court because Reyes was 15 at the time of the shooting.

CEO Diane Phakonekham said Kern County has long been a priority for the organization. The program creates matches between adult volunteers and children ages 6 through 18. Around 10:08 p.m., a man threatened to shoot the reporting party’s husband during a verbal dispute at a Bakersfield apartment complex. No weapon was seen at first, but the same subject was later seen walking through the complex with a baseball bat. Other incidents included a collision near Panama Lane and Ashe Road, a verbal dispute during which a possible gunshot was heard, a physical fight at an apartment on H Street, a trucker on the highway needing CHP to arrange a tow, an attempt to locate a 7-year-old last seen on a residence’s front porch wearing a black shirt, a welfare check on a woman who told bystanders she had been thrown out of a vehicle, medical aid for an unknown complaint on South 8th Street, medical aid for a possible overdose where Narcan was administered, a search for a suspect armed with a switchblade who fled on foot north on Mount Vernon Avenue, medical aid on South Haley Street where interpreters were requested, medical aid for a seizure, and a man on a scooter reportedly armed with a knife — and possibly a gun — last seen near a 711 parking lot in the Olive Drive area.

headline: From Melbourne to Bakersfield: The unlikely match for Bakersfield College's starting quarterback
content:
The Daily Brief

From Melbourne to Bakersfield: The unlikely match for Bakersfield College's starting quarterback

Good morning, Kern County. It’s a mild start to September, with temperatures expected to top out at a comfortable 85 degrees today, but our top story carries some weight: four Bakersfield City Council seats are officially contested for the November ballot, setting up what could be a significant shift in local leadership. We’re also tracking the aftermath of a busy overnight for first responders, including a rollover on Highway 58 and a shots-fired report in the Coburn Ridge area, all while air quality holds at a moderate 57.

The Kern Overnight

It was a steady night for emergency crews across the county as Monday’s heat lingered into the evening and carried a familiar rhythm of calls into the early hours. Just after midnight, a vehicle rollover on westbound Highway 58 west of Tucker Road brought a multi-unit response, including a battalion chief, with an air unit standing by as a precaution. Westbound lanes were reduced while crews worked the scene; the extent of any injuries was not immediately available. Around 1:48 a.m., officers were sent to a residence in the Coburn Ridge area on reports of five to six shots fired, with callers describing subjects in ski masks at the door and a vehicle fleeing the area. The reporting party was checking security cameras as officers responded.

Elsewhere in the county, a grass fire off Wasco Pond Road north of Cecil Avenue drew an engine, a patrol unit, and additional assistance around 1:30 a.m., with crews stopping the fire’s progression and being released from the scene. In north Bakersfield, officers ran a short foot pursuit of a male on a dirt bike along a Chester Avenue bike path, losing visual at Chester Avenue before units began searching the area. Deputies and medics also responded to a residence on Marble Street just before 11 p.m., where a 17-year-old was reported making suicidal statements; family members were contacted. A separate crisis call on West China Grade drew a mental health response, and a domestic disturbance on Meadows Street involving juveniles prompted officers to respond given the concern for children.

The overnight log included a steady stream of lesser calls as well: a small roadside fire on northbound Highway 99 south of Olive Drive, a vehicle fire on Elk Hills Road that turned out to be a dropped flare, a search for a subject in dark clothing last seen heading toward the Mount Vernon Bridge, and a welfare check on a missing 15-year-old last seen near Bernard Street. Crews also handled a court order violation with a firearm threat at Virginia Avenue and Powell Street, and CHP responded to a family member walking on the shoulder of northbound I-5 near the escape ramp. The night was busy, but by sunrise the county had settled into a routine, quieter Tuesday morning.

Today's weather

Expect a pleasant September day with a high near 85 degrees and a low around 58 degrees tonight. It’s currently 72 degrees at Meadows Field (KBFL), with no active weather alerts for Kern County. Air quality is sitting at 57, which is moderate — sensitive individuals may want to take it a bit easier outdoors, but most residents will find conditions just fine. Fire crews are currently monitoring one active fire in Kern, the Rose Fire, so smoke-sensitive folks should stay aware of their local conditions.

Top stories

A local political scientist tells 23ABC that the November election could reshape Bakersfield city leadership, as four council seats — Ward 1, Ward 3, Ward 4, and Ward 7 — each drew at least one challenger against an incumbent. Ward 1’s Eric Arias, Ward 4’s Bob Smith, and Ward 7’s Manpreet Kaur each face a single challenger, while Ward 3 has the most crowded field with six candidates. Councilman Ken Weir is the only sitting member not seeking re-election this season. Political professor Ian Anderson noted that Kern County and Bakersfield tend to lean conservative, a pattern he says may continue in these races, and he highlighted a key detail for first-time voters: city council elections are decided by plurality, not majority, meaning the candidate with the most votes wins outright. Anderson expressed hope the competitive races will drive higher turnout, emphasizing that local elections often affect residents more directly than state or federal contests.

KGET 17 reports that a hit-and-run charge has been filed in the death of a man last October on Camino Media, moving the case one step closer to resolution for a family that has waited nearly a year for accountability. The charge stems from an incident on the street, and prosecutors have now formally brought the case forward. The report does not name the victim or the accused, but the filing signals that investigators have identified a suspect and believe they have enough evidence to proceed. For neighbors along that stretch of road, the news closes a chapter of uncertainty and opens the door to a court process that will determine what happened that night.

According to KGET 17, the Community Action Partnership of Kern is seeing demand for food assistance rise, with the agency’s leadership saying plainly, “We see the need going up.” CAPK, which has long been a backbone of food security efforts in the county, is grappling with increased pressure as families continue to navigate economic strain. The organization is working to meet the moment, but the signal from its leadership is clear: the need is real, it is growing, and community support will be essential to keep pace. For readers who have wondered whether their neighbors are still struggling, the answer from CAPK is an unequivocal yes.

Bakersfield Now reports that crews responded to a drone-like aircraft fire at the Elk Hills-Buttonwillow Airport, a scene that drew a first-alarm response before being handled. The incident involved some type of aircraft with drone-like characteristics, though the full details of what happened and how the fire started remain under investigation. The airport is remote and primarily serves industrial and agricultural traffic, but any fire on an airfield carries inherent risks. That crews contained it quickly is a relief; the investigation into the cause will determine whether this was a mechanical failure, a crash, or something else entirely.

Bakersfield Now also looks at the question of flash flooding in Kern County, turning to the National Weather Service to explain the risk and how residents can stay safe. While the desert and valley are no strangers to dry conditions, the NWS notes that the terrain here can be particularly vulnerable to flash flooding when storms do arrive, especially in burn scars and low-lying crossings. The key message is one of preparedness: know your route, don’t drive through flowing water, and heed warnings when they are issued. It’s a useful primer for a county where rain can be rare but dangerous when it finally comes.

The 23ABC report on the multi-state Salmonella outbreak linked to recalled eggs notes that Kern County has not been impacted locally, according to Kimberly Hernandez with Kern Public Health. The FDA and CDC are investigating 98 infections and 26 hospitalizations across 17 states, including California, with the outbreak linked in part to eggs from Midwest Poultry Services sold under brands like Country Morning, Simple Truth, and Kroger. The recalled eggs carry sell-by or best-by dates between July 20 and Aug. 17. Hernandez said the county has not been made aware of any affected product arriving locally or any connected cases, but she cautioned that travel or secondary distribution could still tie California cases to the outbreak — a reminder that food safety doesn’t always respect state lines.

Something good

One of the more heartening items on the calendar this week is the Spanish Speaking Conference, which KGET 17 reports will connect families with special resources available in the community. The event offers local families a chance to find support, information, and connections in a setting designed to meet them where they are. It’s a reminder that in Bakersfield, help is often just a conversation away — and that the community’s strength is built on neighbors reaching out to neighbors. For families navigating the often-complicated world of special needs services, having a dedicated space like this can make all the difference.

Coming up this week

For those who like to keep an eye on local government, the week ahead has a few gatherings worth noting. The Police Civil Service Commission meets Wednesday, September 2 at 8:30 a.m., and the Personnel and Processes Committee follows later that same day at noon. On Thursday, September 3, the Planning Commission convenes at 5:30 p.m. These are public meetings where decisions get made about the shape of the city — from the makeup of its police oversight to the growth and development that define its future — and residents are welcome to attend in person.

On the entertainment front, the Fox Theater is hosting The Oldies Night: A Night Of Timeless Soul, Doo-Wop, & Classic Oldies this Friday, September 4, followed by Talib Kweli’s One Night Only in Bakersfield on Saturday, September 5. Both are sure to draw a crowd, and they offer a good excuse to enjoy the cooler evening air and support one of downtown’s iconic venues. The following week brings Justin Willman on September 10, Max Amini on September 12, and Clay Walker’s Doin’ What I Love Tour on September 13, so the theater is busy with a little something for every taste.

As you head into the day, take a moment to be good to your neighbors — the overnight calls remind us that a lot of people are carrying heavy loads. Whether that’s a warm greeting, a helping hand, or simply patience in the checkout line, it matters. We’ll be back tomorrow morning with the news you need to start your day.

headline: Local mother calls for answers, joining the fight for cameras in special education classrooms
content:
The Daily Brief

Local mother calls for answers, joining the fight for cameras in special education classrooms

Good morning, Kern County. It's Wednesday, September 2, and while crews are just starting day two of the big Hageman Road construction project that has businesses and commuters bracing for a month of delays, the valley itself is waking up mild and calm — expect a high near 82 today with moderate air quality and no active alerts. There's a lot to get to this morning, from a night of scattered incidents across the county to a deeper look at why the long-predicted wave of baby boomers selling their homes hasn't materialized, so let's get you caught up.

The Kern Overnight

It was a busy but thankfully non-fatal night across Kern County, with the most serious call coming just after midnight on Highway 58. Around 12:41 a.m., a rollover crash on westbound 58 west of Tucker Road drew a multi-unit response including a battalion chief, with an air unit standing by. Westbound lanes were reduced while crews worked the scene, though the extent of any injuries has not been released.

Just over an hour later, at roughly 1:48 a.m., dispatchers sent officers to a home in the Coburn Ridge area on reports of five to six shots fired. Callers said subjects in ski masks had been seen at the door, and the reporting party was pulling camera footage as a vehicle fled the area. Officers responded to the scene.

Elsewhere around the county, crews knocked down a grass fire off Wasco Pond Road north of Cecil Avenue around 1:30 a.m., with fire progression stopped after an engine, patrol unit, and additional help arrived. In Bakersfield, a short foot pursuit of a man on a dirt bike along a Chester Avenue bike path ended around 9:58 p.m. when visual contact was lost near Chester; units were searching the area. Earlier in the evening, a call at Virginia Avenue and Powell Street reported a male subject making threats to obtain a firearm, drawing additional officers to the scene.

The overnight log also included a steady run of welfare checks and mental health calls — a 17-year-old on Marble Street reported making suicidal statements around 10:48 p.m. drew officers and medics, a female in crisis on the West China Grade was attended to around 10:44 p.m., and a welfare check was conducted for a 15-year-old reported missing and last seen near Bernard Street just after midnight. Crews also handled a CHP-reported roadside fire on northbound Highway 99 south of Olive Drive at 9:32 p.m., and a report of a vehicle fire on Elk Hills Road at 11:32 p.m. that turned out to be a dropped flare with no active fire.

Today's weather

It's a mild start to September out there. The current observation at Meadows Field is 61 degrees, with today's high expected to reach only 82 and tonight's low dipping to around 60. There are no active weather alerts for Kern County, and the clear conditions should hold through the day. Air quality sits at 53, which is moderate — fine for most people, though those sensitive to particulates may want to keep outdoor exertion light. Monday's heat has broken, and it looks like a pleasant, seasonable stretch ahead. No active fires are being tracked locally.

Top stories

23ABC reports that a major road construction project on Hageman Road launched Monday at 7 a.m. and will continue daily until 7 p.m. through the end of September. The city says the work is necessary, but businesses along the corridor are already feeling it — a waitress at Slice of Italy told the station customers are struggling to get to the restaurant, and neighboring businesses said they wish the city had given clearer advance notice. Residents, like Tina DiStefano, are worried about traffic congestion and school drop-off delays, while others like Brent Andrews acknowledge the long-anticipated work was inevitable.

KGET 17 reports that the Shafter City Council has approved an ordinance banning sleeping in public. The measure passed amid ongoing debate over how to address homelessness in the small Kern County city. Details on enforcement and any available alternatives for those affected have not been fully detailed, but the vote signals a harder line from local leaders as encampment complaints have risen across the region.

According to 23ABC, the long-predicted "silver tsunami" has never arrived — and that's tightening the housing market for younger Kern County families. Bakersfield Association of Realtors president Paris Davis told the station that many baby boomers are staying in larger homes due to paid-off mortgages, locked-in low interest rates, and the difficulty of downsizing from a 4,000-square-foot house to something smaller. Economics professor Aaron Hegde added that boomers own about 35% of three-bedroom-or-larger homes in the U.S., but he says the bigger driver of high prices is an overall housing shortage, not boomers staying put.

23ABC also reports that Kern County is facing a serious shortage of attorneys, just as California considers expanding access to civil legal help. Greater Bakersfield Legal Assistance calls the county a "legal desert," with only 0.9 attorneys for every 1,000 residents. The organization receives 500 to 700 calls weekly and saw its caseload jump 41% from 2022 to 2025. Kassie Mullican, GBLA's director of community development, said the lack of capacity and funding means more people are navigating civil cases on their own; one client, Mehru Khan, shared that GBLA's help was critical in obtaining a restraining order during a domestic violence situation.

Bakersfield Now reports that two lanes have reopened on southbound I-5 near Grapevine Road. The lanes had been closed following an earlier incident, and CHP confirmed they were back open, which should ease southbound travel through the Grapevine corridor today.

KGET 17 reports on an unlikely new addition to Bakersfield College's football program — a starting quarterback who came all the way from Melbourne, Australia. The story highlights how the Renegades found their signal-caller from halfway around the world, an interesting footnote to the local sports scene as fall practices get underway.

Something good

There's a bit of welcome news in the arts world this week — KGET 17 reports that the Portrait of a Warrior Gallery is moving to a new location and will become a neighbor to Woolworth's next year. It's an exciting new chapter for the gallery and a nice addition to a downtown block that's been growing steadily.

And for something a little different, Bakersfield College's new quarterback literally traveled around the planet to wear a Renegades uniform. It's a reminder that even in a city as rooted in tradition as Bakersfield, the community keeps finding new connections to the wider world — and that local sports can draw talent from anywhere.

Coming up this week

There are a few public meetings worth putting on the calendar. The Police Civil Service Commission meets this morning at 8:30 a.m., and the Personnel and Processes Committee follows at noon — both are open to the public for those keeping an eye on city administration. Looking ahead, the Planning Commission meets tomorrow evening, Thursday, September 3, at 5:30 p.m., which could matter to anyone tracking development proposals across the city and county.

For entertainment, the Fox Theater has a busy run ahead. This Friday, September 4, catch "The Oldies Night: A Night of Timeless Soul, Doo-Wop, & Classic Oldies," followed by Talib Kweli — one night only — on Saturday, September 5. Next week continues with Justin Willman's "One for the Ages Tour" on September 10, Max Amini live in Bakersfield on September 12, and Clay Walker's "Doin' What I Love Tour" on September 13. It's a strong stretch of shows, and with tickets likely to move, it's worth checking the Fox's schedule soon.

Also running through the end of September is that Hageman Road construction — expect daytime delays and plan alternate routes if you travel that corridor, especially during commute hours and school drop-off times. The city says it wants to thank the community for its patience and warns of unannounced delays if unexpected weather occurs.

Have a steady Wednesday, Kern County. Take an extra few minutes on the road, check on your neighbors in the heat-affected corners of the valley, and we'll see you back here tomorrow morning.

headline: California's wildfire funding fee on utility bills leaves some residents unaware of the charge
content:
The Daily Brief

California's wildfire funding fee on utility bills leaves some residents unaware of the charge

Good morning, Kern County. It’s a mild and quiet start to the day, with temperatures sitting near 61 degrees and air quality rated good, but the news is already moving — newly expanded work requirements for CalFresh recipients went into effect this week, a change that could touch tens of thousands of local families. Fire crews remain on two active incidents in the county, though no weather alerts are in effect.

The Kern Overnight

The Kern overnight ran the usual wide span of activity, with one significant call. Just before 3:43 a.m., a grass fire broke out in an open field near Cottonwood Road and East Pacheco Road in east Bakersfield, drawing multiple engines and patrol units to the scene. Firefighters worked the blaze from both flanks, and by about 4:42 a.m. they had its forward spread stopped, allowing additional resources to be canceled. Crews remained on scene for some time afterward to extinguish lingering hot spots.

Earlier, at about 10:27 p.m., a big rig jackknifed and struck the center divider on westbound Highway 58 just east of Broome Avenue. The crash triggered a trauma activation for a person with possible long-bone fractures, and ambulances responded to the location. Around the same time, a passerby reported a transient male assaulting an employee at a downtown business, and officers were sent out.

The early-morning hours brought two separate reports of women possibly being held against their will at area motels. Shortly after 1:30 a.m., a caller told dispatchers a female was believed to be held by a male subject at a motel on South Union Avenue, and officers were sent to check her welfare. Then, around 5:42 a.m., hotel security at a motel in central Bakersfield reported watching a female try to flee a room while a male pulled her back inside. Officers responded to that scene as well.

Elsewhere in the log: a reported overdose on Butte Street drew medical aid at 10:40 p.m. An engine and truck handled an oven fire in central Bakersfield around midnight. Officers investigated after a white four-door hit a curb in the metro area with occupants fleeing on foot at 12:30 a.m. Medics responded for a seizure on Victor Street, a dumpster fire was reported at a market near Panama Lane and Wible Road, and a welfare check was conducted on a suicidal subject at a bus terminal in the White Wolf area. A man in his 30s was found slumped near a motel room on Olive Tree Court, and an exterior trash pile fire near Chester Avenue was quickly handled. In one of the night's brighter moments, paramedics were called just after 5:13 a.m. to the Lakeside Apartments on Panama Lane for an emergency childbirth, with the baby appearing to have been born before medics arrived.

Today's weather

Expect a high near 85 degrees this afternoon with a low around 60 overnight. It's currently 61 degrees at Meadows Field, and there are no active weather alerts for Kern County. Air quality checks in at 35, a "good" reading, so it's a fine day to leave the windows open.

Fire crews, meanwhile, remain on two active wildfires in Kern County: the Triangle Fire and the Knight Fire. Neither is producing any immediate weather-related threat today, but it's worth staying aware of conditions if you're headed into the foothills or mountain areas over the coming days.

Top stories

New work requirements for CalFresh recipients took effect Sept. 1 in Kern County, 23ABC reports, and the rules could put tens of thousands of local cases at risk. Under the policy, certain recipients must now work, attend school, or volunteer at least 20 hours a week to keep their benefits. More than 200,000 people in Kern County — around 100,000 families — rely on CalFresh, and Kelly Lowery with the CAPK Food Bank told the station that as many as 30,000 of those cases could be disenrolled. The food bank is already serving about 50,000 families a month. Lowery said the real challenge isn't a lack of willingness to work, but a lack of jobs that pay a living wage, noting that there simply aren't enough positions paying the $26-an-hour rate that would let two working adults in a household cover their bills. Recipient Veronica Perez, who works 35 hours a week at the food bank, said the requirement isn't a problem for her, but she knows neighbors who struggle with transportation, disabilities, or childcare barriers. More changes arrive Oct. 1, when the federal government increases maximum SNAP benefit amounts for California while adjusting income eligibility limits.

Arvin High School broke ground on a new community school and parent center building, 23ABC reports, a long-awaited project that will expand services for families across the area. The building will house a food pantry, a clothing closet, parent meeting rooms, and space for workshops and classes — resources that currently are crammed into Room 9, a small space that can barely accommodate the demand. Principal Gabriel Ramirez-Leyva told the station the project grew out of years of conversations with parents and students about their greatest needs. Student and Family Support Liaison Adriana Komin said the larger space will allow the school to better serve everyone who walks through its doors, offering a permanent home for efforts like food donation distribution that already reach deep into the community.

A local mother is demanding answers after her autistic 4-year-old son came home from school with bruises, and she's now joining a push for cameras in special education classrooms. According to 23ABC, Jessica Lewis said her son, a student in the Panama Buena Vista School District, returned from school with bruises on his face and no explanation from the school. Lewis said she had to call the school herself and was told only that staff were investigating, with suggestions that the injury might have been an allergic reaction or a bee sting. Her larger concern, she said, is the lack of communication — had her son fallen off a bike and the school called to tell her, she said she'd feel differently. Lewis has connected with mother Ashley Hopwood, who started a petition earlier this year to bring cameras into special needs classrooms, a proposal Lewis now wants her own district to adopt.

KGET 17 reports that a judge is set to rule on whether SEIU Local 521 may join a lawsuit against Bakersfield's sewer rate increases. The union has sought to intervene in the ongoing legal challenge, and the outcome of the hearing will determine whether it can participate in the case as a party. The suit centers on rate hikes approved by the city, which have drawn criticism from residents and advocacy groups who argue the increases place an unfair burden on ratepayers.

Mail thefts in Bakersfield are being linked to black market master keys, according to KGET 17. The keys, which open cluster mailboxes and other centralized delivery units, have become a valuable commodity on underground markets, allowing thieves to bypass locks and steal mail directly from the boxes. Investigators are urging residents to check their mail regularly and report any suspicious activity around neighborhood mailboxes.

Bakersfield police are warning the public about two men who allegedly ask for personal information after staging or approaching car collisions, KGET 17 reports. The men reportedly approach drivers after minor accidents and request personal details under the guise of handling insurance or paperwork. Police advise residents not to share any information at the scene and to contact law enforcement directly if approached in this manner.

Something good

The groundbreaking at Arvin High School is a genuine bright spot for the valley. For years, families have relied on a cramped room to access food, clothing, and guidance — and soon they'll have a dedicated, purpose-built space that treats parents as partners in their children's education. It's the kind of investment that doesn't make headlines elsewhere but changes lives here, one family at a time.

It's also worth a smile that the overnight emergency childbirth at the Panama Lane apartments ended with the baby arriving before medics even reached the room. Congratulations to the new parents — you're the second good story from the night shift.

Coming up this week

If you want to shape the city's future, the place to be is the Bakersfield Planning Commission meeting, scheduled for Thursday, Sept. 3, at 5:30 p.m. The commission's agenda covers land-use and development items that will influence the look and feel of the city for years to come, and public comment is typically welcome. Check the city's website for the full agenda and attendance details.

For a weekend of music, the Fox Theater has you covered. On Friday, Sept. 4, catch *The Oldies Night*, an evening of timeless soul, doo-wop, and classic oldies. On Saturday, Sept. 5, hip-hop artist Talib Kweli performs his one-night-only Bakersfield show, followed later in the week by Justin Willman's "One for the Ages" tour on Sept. 10, Max Amini live on Sept. 12, and Clay Walker's "Doin' What I Love Tour" on Sept. 13. If you're a regular at the Fox, the 2026-2027 Cults & Classics Season Pass is already on sale — a full season of the theater's most distinctive programming.

Beyond the Fox, keep an eye on school district calendars and city advisory boards, as the new school year brings a full slate of regular meetings in the coming days. As always, check with the individual hosts before heading out, as dates and times can shift.

headline: Harrington House restaurant in SW Bakersfield to close
content:
The Daily Brief

Harrington House restaurant in SW Bakersfield to close

Good morning, Kern County. It's Friday, September 4th, and we're waking up to a mild start with a high near 85 degrees today — perfect weather for easing into the holiday weekend. Our top story is the local reaction to the passing of feminist icon Gloria Steinem, whose six-decade friendship with Dolores Huerta left a profound mark here in the valley. Air quality is good this morning, no active weather alerts, and firefighters continue to watch the Dove Fire.

The Kern Overnight

The night was busier than the quiet weather suggested, with the Kern County Sheriff's Office and Bakersfield police handling a string of incidents that stretched from the west side of the city out toward the high desert.

The most significant call came just before 9:30 p.m., when a driver refused to yield and led officers northbound along Madison Street. The pursuit stretched past 10 o'clock, with speeds reaching roughly 55 mph on roadways that were otherwise empty of traffic and pedestrians. Units picked up the chase after the initial stop was refused, and there was a brief concern over a possible gunshot before the pursuit continued north.

Around 2:55 a.m., deputies and medical units responded to a home near Bluestone Riverway for a domestic assault with a weapon. A man was accused of attacking his girlfriend with scissors and throwing a vase at her hand during a dispute, leaving minor injuries. Juveniles were present at the residence, and one reportedly had a nosebleed; a caller disputed a claim that one of the juveniles was pregnant.

Just after 12:26 a.m., reports of smoke coming from a building near Edwards Air Force Base pulled a large fire assignment — multiple engines and a battalion chief. Crews arrived to find only light residual smoke reaching into the attic, cancelled the reinforcements, and scaled the response back to a regular structure fire.

Minutes later, around 12:37 a.m., an employee watching live surveillance footage saw two hooded males force their way into a business on 15th Street West and begin taking items. The employee then lost connection to the cameras — possibly because the suspects had removed them — and units began clearing the area.

Earlier in the evening, a domestic call on East 21st Street turned urgent around 11:40 p.m. when a caller could be heard yelling in the background before the suspect began chasing her. Officers responded to the area, where the caller reported being struck near 21st and D Street. The overnight log also included a possible DUI involving a white service truck swerving after exiting the freeway around 9:20 p.m., an outside fire on E Street at 9:53 p.m., a welfare check on St. Mary's Street involving a juvenile who said an older brother had choked him, and a 2:13 a.m. call from a woman who said a man had tried to strangle her during a verbal dispute.

Today's weather

Expect a mostly clear day with a high near 85° and a low around 63° tonight. It's currently 63° at Meadows Field, with no active weather alerts for Kern County. Air quality is good at an AQI of 40, so it's a fine morning for a walk or an open window. Fire crews are watching one active fire in Kern County — the Dove Fire — as conditions remain mild and favorable.

Top stories

KGET 17 reports that local Navy veterans are reflecting on the USS Abraham Lincoln's record-long deployment, which stretched over 200 days at sea. Veterans in Kern County who served on the carrier told the station the deployment was grueling, with one describing it as "miserable" for the crew and their families. The Lincoln's extended time away has renewed conversation about the strain such long deployments place on service members and the people waiting for them at home.

According to 23ABC, six candidates are running for seats on the Arvin City Council ahead of Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and two of them recently sat down to share their priorities. Anabel Quintino Rubio, an Arvin native who went through the city's school system, said her focus is on improving the city's finances and working as a team to get Arvin out of its deficit. Nora Perez, who grew up in Arvin after her family moved from Los Angeles, emphasized development — streets, gutters, curbs, and making the downtown look nice — and said she wants a better Arvin for the next generation.

KGET 17 reports that Shafter has adopted a "no public sleeping" law, a decision that comes as the city reports just five homeless individuals. The ordinance prohibits sleeping in public spaces, and city officials say it's a tool to address concerns while connecting people with services. Critics may question the necessity given the small number, but the council moved forward with the measure.

Bakersfield Now reports that an investigation has found a Bakersfield College athlete continued playing after a restraining order was issued against him. The outlet's reporting raises questions about how the college and its athletic department handled the situation, and whether policies were followed. The investigation highlights ongoing concerns about accountability and safety in college sports programs.

23ABC is reporting that Gloria Steinem's death Wednesday at age 92 has prompted reflection in Kern County on her six-decade friendship with Dolores Huerta. The two met in 1967 while Huerta was in New York leading the national table-grape boycott, and Steinem became a strong supporter of the farmworkers movement. Camila Chavez, executive director of the Dolores Huerta Foundation, said Steinem's death is the loss of a "shero of the movement" who helped bridge workers' rights and women's rights across generations.

According to KGET 17, a man was cited for hit-and-run after multiple crashes in Bear Valley Springs. The incidents caused property damage but no reported injuries, and the man was located and cited by deputies. The case is a reminder of the importance of staying at the scene, even in minor collisions.

Something good

This week's Wag Wednesday introduced Bobert, a Frenchie mix with a face that's hard to resist, and he's currently looking for his forever home here in Kern County. The feature gives the community a warm opportunity to meet a hopeful pet each week — and for someone, maybe, to welcome a new four-legged family member before the weekend begins. If you've been thinking about adding a dog to your life, Bobert might be worth a visit.

Coming up this week

The Fox Theater has a busy stretch ahead. Tonight, Friday, Sept. 4, the historic venue on H Street hosts The Oldies Night — A Night of Timeless Soul, Doo-Wop & Classic Oldies, a trip back through the golden era of music. Saturday brings Talib Kweli for a one-night-only show in Bakersfield, and next week continues with Justin Willman's "One for the Ages" tour on Thursday, Sept. 10, Max Amini live on Saturday, Sept. 12, and Clay Walker's "Doin' What I Love" tour on Sunday, Sept. 13. With everything from hip-hop to country and comedy on the calendar, there's something for just about every taste. For anyone planning ahead, the theater's Season Pass for 2026–2027 is also available, covering the full lineup of films and shows coming through town in the months ahead.

headline: Volunteers prep for Greek Food Festival with new dishes, chance to win trip to Greece
content:
The Daily Brief

Volunteers prep for Greek Food Festival with new dishes, chance to win trip to Greece

Good morning, Kern County. Saturday starts with sober news: a police pursuit in North Bakersfield ended overnight when the suspect vehicle struck and killed a pedestrian on a sidewalk, and two men are in custody. The weather is mild for early September — highs near 89 — but air quality is moderate, so take it easy if you're sensitive. We'll walk you through the overnight reports and what to know for the week ahead.

The Kern Overnight

Shortly after 1:30 a.m., Bakersfield Police officers with the Special Enforcement Unit tried to arrest a man wanted on a Ramey warrant near Clover Mountain Court and Pine Meadow Drive. The suspect climbed into the passenger side of a waiting car, and when the driver refused to stop, officers began a pursuit that ran south on Airport Drive, reaching speeds of 91 mph. At the intersection with Olive Drive, officers deployed spike strips. The driver swerved, lost control, and plowed into an adult man standing on the west sidewalk. Paramedics performed CPR, but the pedestrian was pronounced dead at the scene. The two men inside the car fled on foot but were caught quickly; both were taken to a hospital for medical clearance before booking. The California Highway Patrol is investigating the crash.

Elsewhere, fire crews were busy throughout the night. A man with a shopping cart was reported lighting a string of small fires along East California Avenue, with separate blazes near Haley Street and Williams Street. Investigators are treating the case as arson. A brush fire near Pozo Creek and the Granite area grew to 15 to 20 acres and drew a large Kern County assignment that included engines, a strike team and a type-2 helicopter; crews had to reach the flames through ranch gates and dirt roads. A report of a gunshot wound near Acres Road and Barbara Avenue sent emergency medical units to stage, with officers positioned nearby. On northbound Interstate 5 just south of the split, a crash involving up to three vehicles left cars in the center divider and shut down the freeway while rescue crews worked. The rest of the overnight log was a mix of the usual: a vehicle-versus-bicycle collision on White Lane between Monitor and Union avenues, a domestic dispute on Chester Lane, copper theft in the Bell Terrace area where utility poles were being cut down, a street takeover of roughly 30 vehicles in a Colony Drive parking lot, a panic alarm on Adelaide Avenue, and a fire along the railroad tracks south of East Truxton Avenue. Dry conditions kept engines rolling, and no rain is in the forecast.

Today's weather

Expect a high near 89° under sunny skies, with a low around 65° overnight. At this hour, Meadows Field is already at 86°. There are no active weather alerts for Kern County, and the air quality index is 54 — moderate, so keep that in mind if you're prone to breathing issues. No major fires are threatening the valley, and the brush fire near Pozo Creek is the one to watch. No rain is expected through the weekend, and the fire danger will stay elevated in the hills.

Top stories

23ABC reports that one man is dead and two others are in custody following a police chase that ended on Airport Drive near Olive Drive. The pursuit began around 1:30 a.m. when the Bakersfield Police Department's Special Enforcement Unit tried to arrest a 21-year-old suspect wanted on a Ramey warrant for firearm possession and gang-related charges. Officers spotted him near Clover Mountain Court and Pine Meadow Drive, but he climbed into the passenger side of a car driven by a 20-year-old, and the driver took off. As the car traveled south on Airport Drive, officers deployed spike strips at the intersection with Olive Drive. The driver swerved, lost control, and struck an unidentified adult male pedestrian on the west sidewalk, killing him. Both suspects ran but were quickly caught; police say a minor use of force was involved, and both were transported to a hospital for medical clearance. The California Highway Patrol is handling the crash investigation.

KGET 17 reports that the City of Maricopa will consider installing two Flock cameras. The item is headed for a city council meeting, according to the station. Flock cameras are automated license plate readers that can alert law enforcement when a vehicle linked to a crime rolls past. For a small town like Maricopa, the decision is a significant step into surveillance technology — and it raises the usual questions about privacy versus public safety. Exact locations for the cameras haven't been shared, and the meeting date hasn't been announced, so residents who want to weigh in should keep an eye on the city's agenda.

Bakersfield Now reports that a local attorney says BPD's warning about men approaching crash scenes fits the profile of "cappers." The department recently cautioned residents about people showing up after accidents and offering services. The lawyer says that behavior matches the description of "cappers" — individuals who solicit accident victims for business, often without proper licensing. His advice is to stay in your car, call police, and avoid making agreements with anyone you didn't ask for. It's a helpful reminder that not everyone who stops at the scene of a wreck is there to lend a hand.

KGET 17 also reports that Harrington House, a restaurant in southwest Bakersfield, is closing its doors. The eatery, known for its comfort-food menu, shared the news with customers but hasn't announced an exact closing date or a future plan. The closure is a loss for the local dining scene, and regulars are already planning one last visit. We'll follow this one and let you know if the space gets a new tenant.

Something good

Something good to carry into the weekend: music is filling classrooms again across the Bakersfield City School District, thanks to Proposition 28 funding. The measure, passed by voters three years ago, sends an estimated $800 million to $1 billion a year to arts and music education. At Myra Noble Elementary, a second grader says music class has made it easier to talk with her teacher and classmates, and her teacher hopes students carry a passion for creativity with them. Another music teacher at Jefferson Elementary says hearing piano chords ignites listening skills right away. District officials also report a practical benefit: students in music programs have higher attendance than their non-music peers, and they're working to build that same momentum at the elementary level.

Coming up this week

Coming up this week, the Fox Theater has a lineup worth planning around. On Thursday, Sept. 10, Justin Willman brings his "One for the Ages" tour to the stage, blending comedy and magic. Saturday, Sept. 12, comedian Max Amini performs live in Bakersfield. Sunday, Sept. 13, country favorite Clay Walker rolls through on his "Doin' What I Love" tour. For film buffs, the Cults & Classics series continues Monday, Sept. 14, with a screening of "Fargo." Then on Friday, Sept. 18, it's a 2000s party to close out the week. If comedy is more your speed, Jeff Richards and William Montgomery are booked at The Well Comedy Club — check the club's listings for show times. On the public-agenda side, the Maricopa City Council is expected to take up the two Flock cameras this week, though no date has been announced in the materials we received, so check the city's agenda before heading out. No other major public meetings have been announced for Kern County in the coming days, but agendas can change — a quick call to the city or county clerk can save you a wasted trip. Whether you're into magic, country, comedy or a classic film, there's a way to end the week in Kern County.

headline: 8-year-old Bakersfield boxer is already 6-0 with three titles to his name
content:
The Daily Brief

8-year-old Bakersfield boxer is already 6-0 with three titles to his name

Good morning, Kern County. It's Sunday, September 6, and the story shaping the day is a heavy one: Bakersfield police are investigating the death of a pedestrian struck during a high-speed pursuit in North Bakersfield early Saturday, with two suspects in custody. The weather, at least, is offering a gentler note — 72 degrees at Meadows Field, a high near 86, no weather alerts and no active fires — a fine close to the Labor Day weekend.

The Kern Overnight

It was an active night across Kern County, with law enforcement and fire crews moving from one call to the next from the north end of Bakersfield to the far edges of the county. Officers with helicopter support chased two subjects who fled on foot across a property near Golden State Avenue in north Bakersfield, setting up a perimeter as the search stretched into the early hours. A separate foot pursuit wound through residential yards near Decatur Avenue, where officers boxed the suspect in between two fenced properties and brought the chase to an end.

In eastern Kern, crews responded to a pair of vehicles that struck power poles in the span of the night. One vehicle left the roadway and hit a pole in a vineyard off King Street, shearing it and bringing down power lines; another rolled onto its roof after crashing into a pole along Edison Highway just west of the main corridor, drawing a combined response from fire and law enforcement. Utility crews were left to sort out the damaged lines as the scenes were cleared.

Firefighters also spent the early hours on a vegetation fire burning on both sides of the railroad tracks and riverbed just east of Golden State Avenue, with crews sent in to knock it down before it could spread. In the Fremont Street area on the south end of the street, multiple units responded to a fire at an apartment complex, and fire crews were dispatched to a reported vehicle fire on Highway 99 just north of 7th Standard Road in the south county.

Two other calls kept officers busy through the night, both ending without injury. On Pacheco Road in south Bakersfield, a person reported to be armed with a knife was located in an alley area; the weapon was found and the situation was resolved peacefully. In the 18th Street area, a possible intoxicated driver fled a location after claiming to have a firearm, last seen heading southbound, with units searching the area.

Today's weather

It's a comfortable 72 degrees right now at Meadows Field, and the valley should climb to a high near 86 this afternoon before settling to a low around 64 tonight. There are no active weather alerts for Kern County, air quality reports are not posting a reading, and no active fires are burning in the region.

One thing to keep in mind for the rest of the holiday weekend: Bakersfield Now reports that forecasters are staying "weather aware" through Labor Day as moisture from Hurricane Marie could work its way into the region. Nothing is set in stone, but it's worth keeping an eye on the sky if your Monday plans take you outside.

Top stories

A bystander was killed early Saturday morning when a car being pursued by police lost control on Airport Drive and struck him, KGET 17 reports, and two suspects are in custody. According to 23ABC, Bakersfield police were trying to arrest 21-year-old Isaiah Andrade — wanted on a Ramey warrant for firearm possession and gang-related charges — when he climbed into the passenger side of a vehicle driven by 20-year-old Gabriel Lopez, who refused to stop. Officers deployed spike strips as the car traveled south on Airport Drive; in an apparent attempt to avoid them, the driver lost control and hit the pedestrian on the west sidewalk, where he was pronounced dead. Both Lopez and Andrade fled on foot from the crash but were quickly captured.

The Kern Autism Network marked its 30th anniversary Saturday at the Bakersfield Country Club, according to 23ABC, celebrating an organization that started as a parent support group in 1996 and has grown into a source of education, community events and support groups for families across Kern County. President Bernard Puget told 23ABC he and his wife Ramona became involved about 25 years ago after doctors warned that their young son could one day be institutionalized — a future they refused to accept, and one that led them to help other families find their footing. Board member Grant Davenport said the network's support groups now serve women, families and adults, and the milestone did not go unrecognized: Mayor Karen Goh presented a certificate, and a representative from Congressman David Valadao's office offered a plaque.

The city of Maricopa is set to consider installing two Flock cameras, KGET 17 reported, a proposal that would bring the automated license-plate reading technology to the small southwest Kern community. The item is headed for consideration before city leaders, a sign that the region's network of the cameras continues to grow as local agencies weigh their use in investigations.

Volunteers from St. George Greek Orthodox Church are deep into prep work for this year's Greek Food Festival, 23ABC reported, with about 10 cooks working since 8 a.m. on family recipes passed down through generations. Mother and daughter Liz Rodgers and Ariel Munoz told 23ABC the event has been a family tradition for 40 years; the rice pilaf they were preparing came from Rodgers' Greek in-laws. New this year are feta bites — pieces of feta coated, fried and drizzled with honey — along with raffle tickets for a trip to Greece. Volunteer Irene Sinopole said roughly 5,000 people attended last year, and the church expects that number to grow.

Something good

There are a couple of things worth smiling about in Kern County this weekend. The Kern Autism Network's three decades is one of them — an anniversary that started with parents refusing to accept a bleak prognosis and turned into a community standing beside other families walking the same road. The Greek Food Festival volunteers are the other: 40 years of cooking, dancing and sharing culture with the whole county, with the rice pilaf already prepared and frozen, ready to be brought back to life for the crowds. It's the kind of week where the best of the valley is on full display.

Coming up this week

Monday is Labor Day, the last day of the long weekend, and the last chance to enjoy the summer weather before the week settles in — though that Hurricane Marie moisture from the forecast is worth watching for holiday plans.

Looking at the week ahead at the Fox Theater, there's a full slate: Justin Willman brings his One for the Ages Tour on Thursday, Sept. 10; comedian Max Amini performs live on Saturday, Sept. 12; and Clay Walker's Doin' What I Love Tour takes the stage on Sunday, Sept. 13. The Cults & Classics series continues Monday, Sept. 14 with a screening of Fargo, and the theater closes out the stretch with It's a 2000s Party on Friday, Sept. 18.

For those keeping an eye on local government, Maricopa city leaders have the two-camera Flock proposal on a coming agenda, as KGET 17 reported, and the Greek Food Festival is drawing closer by the day as the volunteers keep cooking. It's a full week ahead — enjoy the holiday, stay cool, and keep the radio on.

headline: Preliminary hearing in North Kern State Prison homicide postponed to January
content:
The Daily Brief

Preliminary hearing in North Kern State Prison homicide postponed to January

Good morning, Kern County — it’s Monday, September 7, 2026, and the long Labor Day weekend is winding down under a warm, clear sky. The news leading the day is an Amber Alert that now reaches into Kern County, with CHP asking drivers to watch for a white Nissan Altima without plates, while KGET 17 is also reporting a fatal shooting in McFarland. Expect a high near 93, air quality in the good range at 48, and no active weather alerts or fire advisories on the board.

The Kern Overnight

The last night of the holiday weekend was a mostly quiet one for dispatchers, though firework complaints kept crews checking neighborhoods into the early hours. The most dramatic call came shortly before 10 p.m., when residents near La Cresta Avenue reported a loud blast strong enough to shake doors open. Multiple neighbors phoned in the same boom, and responders treated it as a firework report rather than something more serious.

Two calls drew the biggest responses of the night. In the early hours, deputies were sent to a rural property near 230th Street and Gaskell Avenue after three people in dark clothing were reported cutting through a chain-link fence toward heavy equipment and storage sheds. The group was described as having arrived in a pickup and an SUV pulling flatbed trailers. In northwest Bakersfield, a property owner reported that a white 2018 Freightliner semi truck had been stolen, telling officers a firearm was inside the cab when it was taken.

Just before midnight, a two-vehicle collision left both cars off the roadway; no injuries were reported, and one driver was taken into custody on suspicion of driving under the influence. The rest of the overnight log was routine: a vehicle struck a horse along Wheeler Ridge Road and left the scene, a man in dark clothing was reported in the median on Union Avenue yelling threats while holding a piece of sheet metal, a masked person was caught on surveillance near North Chester Avenue, and officers checked on a woman near Jefferson Park after a friend reported hearing impact sounds during a call.

Today's weather

Forecasters expect a high near 93 today and a low around 69 tonight. The current reading at Meadows Field is 70 degrees, so it will warm up quickly but stay comfortable by September standards. No active weather alerts are posted for Kern County.

Air quality is good, with the index at 48. No active fire information was listed in this morning's briefing, leaving the valley with a clear, calm start to the week.

Top stories

KGET 17 reports that one person is dead after a shooting in McFarland. Police are investigating the shooting, and the morning report offered no word on a suspect or arrest. It is a somber start to the week for the small Kern County community.

According to 23ABC, an Amber Alert issued Sunday extends into Kern County and 10 other California counties. The CHP believes a 14-year-old girl reported missing in Salinas is with a 38-year-old man, and that the pair is traveling in a white Nissan Altima without license plates. The Monterey County Sheriff's Office said arrest warrants were issued last month in connection with the death of an infant.

A Bakersfield man was held to answer on charges alleging sexual abuse of an 8-year-old girl, KGET 17 reported. Being held to answer means a judge found enough evidence for the case to move forward. The report did not name the man or give a next court date.

23ABC reported that Kern Behavioral Health and Recovery Services will host its second annual 988 Day Resource Fair and Blood Drive on Tuesday at Beale Memorial Library. The event runs from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. and includes suicide prevention resources, safety plan training, coping workbooks and a blood drive with Houchin Community Blood Bank. The local 988 team has answered more than 40,000 calls, chats and texts over the past year, more than 7,000 of them involving current or past suicidal thoughts.

The Kern County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's help as it investigates a May shooting on Eucalyptus Drive, KGET 17 said. Beyond the request for information, the morning report included no additional detail. Investigators are hoping someone with knowledge of the case will come forward.

Something good

One bright spot this morning comes from the boxing gym. 23ABC has the story of Jayd Soto, an 8-year-old Bakersfield boxer who is already 6-0 with three titles, including the Junior Olympics and Junior Golden Gloves. He trains five days a week at Warmup Athletics under professional boxer Joel Iriarte, who says Jayd picks up technique quickly — especially the "step back two" that sets up a standing eight count.

And for anyone looking ahead to the next community gathering, volunteers are already preparing for the Greek Food Festival, which will feature new dishes and a chance to win a trip to Greece. It's a joyful reason for the valley to come together, and more details should be coming soon.

Coming up this week

The week's calendar is light on public meetings but rich with things to do. On Tuesday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., the 988 Day Resource Fair and Blood Drive will be at Beale Memorial Library, offering suicide prevention resources, safety plan training and a chance to donate blood with Houchin Community Blood Bank. September is Suicide Prevention Awareness Month, and the fair pairs with a month-long library partnership that includes mental health resources and a curated book list.

At the Fox Theater, the season continues with the Cults & Classics Season Pass for 2026-2027 already on sale. This Thursday, Justin Willman brings his One for the Ages Tour to town, followed by Max Amini live in Bakersfield on Saturday and Clay Walker's Doin' What I Love Tour on Sunday. Next Monday, the Cults & Classics series screens Fargo, and the following Friday closes the week with an It's A 2000s Party. If the holiday left room on the calendar, there are plenty of ways to fill it.
